hero.title: Prompt à Écouter
hero.subtitle: Pratiquer l'Art d'Écouter
hero.description: Une plateforme communautaire christadelphienne pour pratiquer l'art d'écouter. Rejoignez-nous pour retrouver la discipline spirituelle d'une écoute attentive et compatissante à travers notre pratique de conversation en trois parties.

james.text: Que tout homme soit prompt à écouter, lent à parler, lent à se mettre en colère.

proverbs18.text: Celui qui répond avant d'avoir écouté fait un acte de folie et s'attire la confusion.

proverbs20.text: Les intentions dans le cœur de l'homme sont des eaux profondes, mais l'homme intelligent y puise.

timothy.text: Il faut que le serviteur du Seigneur ne soit pas querelleur, mais qu'il soit affable pour tous, propre à enseigner, doué de patience.

ecclesiastes.text: Prends garde à ton pied, lorsque tu entres dans la maison de Dieu ; approche-toi pour écouter, plutôt que pour offrir le sacrifice des insensés.

listeningDeficit.title: Un déficit d'écoute
listeningDeficit.content: Nous vivons à une époque où tout le monde parle, mais peu écoutent vraiment. Les réseaux sociaux récompensent les réactions rapides plutôt que la réflexion réfléchie. Les débats se concentrent sur la victoire plutôt que sur la compréhension. Même dans nos communautés de foi, nous pouvons nous retrouver à parler sans nous écouter, défendant des positions plutôt qu'explorant la vérité ensemble. Ce n'est pas seulement un problème de communication—c'est spirituel. Quand nous n'écoutons pas bien, nous ratons l'opportunité d'aimer bien.

practising.title: Pratiquer l'Art d'Écouter
practising.intro: Nous développons une pratique simple pour aider à retrouver cet art perdu. Elle implique trois personnes en conversation, chacune prenant un rôle spécifique :

speaker.title: L'Orateur
speaker.description: partage ce qu'il a sur le cœur sans interruption

listener.title: L'Auditeur
listener.description: reflète ce qu'il a entendu, sans ajouter ses propres pensées

scribe.title: Le Scribe
scribe.description: capture les idées clés et aide le groupe à se souvenir de ce qui a été partagé

practising.rotation: Les rôles tournent, pour que chacun expérimente parler, écouter et observer. Ce n'est pas de la thérapie ou du conseil—c'est une pratique d'attention, de patience et de soin.
practising.updated: Cette pratique crée un espace pour le type d'écoute qui permet aux gens d'être vraiment entendus. Elle ralentit notre impulsion à répondre et crée de l'espace pour une compréhension plus profonde. Il ne s'agit pas d'accord—il s'agit d'attention. Il ne s'agit pas de résoudre des problèmes—il s'agit de créer les conditions où la sagesse peut émerger et les relations peuvent s'approfondir.

guideCta.title: Want to learn more about these roles?
guideCta.description: Download our detailed guide to understand each role deeply and prepare for meaningful conversations.

format.title: Pourquoi utiliser ce format ?
format.intro: Ce format d'écoute est exactement cela—un outil pour pratiquer et intégrer des valeurs intemporelles :

humility.title: Humilité
humility.verse: Ne faites rien par esprit de parti ou par vaine gloire, mais que l'humilité vous fasse regarder les autres comme étant au-dessus de vous-mêmes.

mutualSubmission.title: Soumission Mutuelle
mutualSubmission.verse: Vous soumettant les uns aux autres dans la crainte de Christ.

attentiveListening.title: Écoute Attentive
attentiveListening.verse: Que tout homme soit prompt à écouter, lent à parler, lent à se mettre en colère.

drawingWisdom.title: Puiser la Sagesse
drawingWisdom.verse: Les intentions dans le cœur de l'homme sont des eaux profondes, mais l'homme intelligent y puise.

pitfalls.title: Elle nous aide aussi à nous prémunir contre les pièges courants :

items.reactiveness: Réactivité et débat : L'Auditeur ne répond pas, mais reflète ce qu'il a entendu.
items.dominance: Dominance et statut : Les rôles tournent—personne ne reste en charge.
items.losingInsight: Perdre la perspicacité : Le Scribe aide à capturer ce qui pourrait autrement être oublié ou négligé.

format.grounding: Cette structure est une méthode moderne, mais en testant son esprit—discernant si elle s'aligne avec la sagesse divine—nous la trouvons fondée dans l'Écriture. Nous ne cherchons pas la nouveauté pour elle-même, mais de nouvelles façons de devenir ce que nous sommes appelés à être : un peuple façonné par l'amour, la sagesse et un soin mutuel profond.
format.discernment: Certains peuvent s'inquiéter qu'une écoute attentive nous ouvre à des idées nuisibles ou trompeuses. Mais écouter n'est pas être d'accord. L'erreur d'Adam n'était pas d'écouter Ève—c'était d'obéir contre le commandement de Dieu. À travers l'Écriture, le peuple de Dieu est appelé à discerner, pas à rejeter ; à tester l'esprit de ce qui est dit, pas à craindre de l'entendre. L'écoute crée l'espace pour un tel discernement. L'enquête nous aide à entendre plus exactement ce qui est dit—si souvent nous réagissons non pas à ce qui a vraiment été dit, mais à un malentendu. La pratique de l'écoute attentive nous ralentit et donne de l'espace pour la clarification, prévenant les conflits inutiles et aidant le corps à grandir dans la vérité et l'amour.

rootedInWord.title: Enraciné dans la Parole
rootedInWord.content: Nous fondons cette approche dans l'Écriture. Nous croyons qu'écouter n'est pas seulement une compétence de communication ; c'est une pratique spirituelle. Elle s'aligne avec la douceur et la patience que Paul a exhortées dans 2 Timothée. Elle crée les conditions où nous pouvons corriger sans quereller, et enseigner sans orgueil. C'est le sol dans lequel l'amour, la patience et la tolérance mutuelle peuvent grandir.

hero.subtitle: Good conversations need more than good intentions. They need people who know how to listen.
hero.description: A practice for slowing down, hearing one another clearly, and discovering what emerges when we listen with care.

presence.title: Be present
presence.text: Give someone your full attention before you decide what to say next.

patience.title: Slow down
patience.text: Quick replies often miss the point. Space to hear creates clearer thinking.

curiosity.title: Stay curious
curiosity.text: Ask what someone means, not how to win the exchange.

clarity.title: Reflect accurately
clarity.text: Check you understood before you challenge, advise, or move on.

humility.title: Hold your view lightly
humility.text: Your perspective matters—and so does the possibility that you do not see everything yet.

introduction.content: Most of us were taught to speak with confidence. Fewer of us were taught to listen with skill. In workplaces, friendships, families, and communities, conversation often rewards the quickest answer, the sharpest point, or the loudest voice. This practice offers a different pace: one that makes room for understanding before reaction.

listeningDeficit.title: A listening deficit
listeningDeficit.content1: We live with a quiet pressure to know, to teach, and to respond immediately. That pressure shows up as interruption, defensiveness, and conversations that leave everyone feeling unseen. Answering before listening is common—and costly.
listeningDeficit.content2: The result is familiar: people talk past each other about important things. Relationships fray. Good ideas go unheard. Conflict hardens because nobody felt properly received.

practising.title: Practising the art of listening
practising.intro1: Listening well is not passive silence. It is active, compassionate attention—the kind that slows us down, draws people out, and creates space for insight none of us could reach alone.
practising.intro2: The practice centres on three rotating roles:

speaker.description: Shares what's on their mind, taking time to explore their thoughts and feelings.

listener.description: Offers full attention and reflects back what they heard, without adding advice or their own agenda.

scribe.description: Captures key insights and themes, helping the group remember what was shared.

guideCta.title: Want to learn more about these roles?
guideCta.description: Download our guide to understand each role and prepare for meaningful conversations.

practising.rotation: These roles rotate. Everyone becomes a speaker, a listener, and a scribe. No one stays in charge of the outcome. Instead, we trust what can emerge when people listen carefully together—drawing out not only words, but the meaning beneath them.
practising.discovery: As the conversation unfolds, it often leads to discoveries none of us could have reached alone. Our understanding is always partial. Through mutual listening, we begin to notice blind spots and assumptions that only another person's attention can help illuminate.
practising.trust: This practice is not about controlling the conversation. It is about trusting the process: patience, accurate reflection, and room for people to revise their own thinking when they feel heard.

format.intro1: The Speaker–Listener–Scribe structure is a practical tool. It helps people live out values that make hard conversations safer and more useful.
format.intro2: This listening format helps enact values such as:

humility.title: Humility
humility.text: Treat other people's experience as worth careful attention, not as an obstacle to your point.

mutualCare.title: Mutual care
mutualCare.text: Share the work of speaking and listening so no one carries the whole conversation alone.

attentiveListening.title: Attentive listening
attentiveListening.text: Be quick to hear and slower to speak—especially when you feel sure you already know.

drawingOut.title: Drawing things out
drawingOut.text: Help people find the meaning under their first words, rather than debating the surface.

pitfalls.title: It also helps guard against common pitfalls:

items.reactiveness: Reactiveness and debate: the Listener does not reply with their own view, but reflects what they heard.
items.dominance: Dominance and status: the roles rotate—no one stays in charge.
items.losingInsight: Losing insight: the Scribe helps capture what might otherwise be forgotten.

format.grounding: This structure is a modern method, but its spirit is simple: create conditions where people can hear one another, test ideas carefully, and stay in relationship while they do.

items.trust: Having been heard, people are more likely to receive challenge later. Trust comes before correction.
items.selfCorrection: Ideas are drawn out more fully, so flaws often become visible to the speaker themselves.
items.smallGroups: Small groups let people explore without performing for a crowd.
items.scribing: Reflection and notes keep clarity, so useful insights—and weak claims—are harder to lose.
items.pace: A slower pace and rotating roles encourage discernment instead of reactive misunderstanding.
items.timeLimits: Time limits keep balance, so no single voice overwhelms the group.

whyItMatters.title: Why it matters
whyItMatters.content: Listening is not only a communication skill. It is a practice of respect. It creates the conditions for disagreement without contempt, for learning without humiliation, and for conversations sturdy enough to hold complexity.

hero.subtitle: Churches are called to speak the truth in love. But how can we speak the truth in love if we have not first learned to listen?
hero.description: A listening practice for churches and faith communities—recovering attentive, compassionate conversation through Speaker, Listener, and Scribe.

james1.text: Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.

proverbs18.text: If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame.

corinthians.text: I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh… For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh?

timothy.text: The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness.

ecclesiastes.text: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.

introduction.content: It is easy to forget how deeply Scripture values listening. In our culture—and often in church conversations—there is a quiet pressure to be the one who knows, who teaches, who speaks with confidence. Scripture pushes us toward a different wisdom: not the quick retort, but the attentive ear.

listeningDeficit.title: A listening deficit
listeningDeficit.content1: The Proverbs warn of the folly of answering before listening. James reminds us that hearing must come before speaking, and that anger—often the fruit of defensive or unchecked speech—does not produce the righteousness of God. Paul, writing to Corinth, describes a church fractured by immaturity—strife, factions, jealousy—and marks these as symptoms of people still driven by the flesh rather than the Spirit.
listeningDeficit.content2: It is not difficult to see parallels in our own communities. We share faith and a love of Scripture, yet we also know the pain of fractured conversations—over doctrine, relationships, or church practice—where we speak past one another.

practising.title: Practising the art of listening
practising.intro1: If we are to become mature in Christ, we must recover the art of listening—not passive silence, but active, compassionate attention. The kind of listening that Jesus often invited through his poetic and enigmatic statements. His parables, questions, and open-ended encounters called others to listen more deeply—to themselves, to him, and to the movement of God in their lives. This kind of listening slows us down, draws us out, and opens a space where Wisdom might speak.
practising.intro2: To that end, this practice helps congregations and small groups listen better and trust the conversation. It centres around three roles:

speaker.description: Shares what's on their heart, taking time to explore their thoughts and feelings.

listener.description: Offers full attention and reflects back what they heard, without adding their own thoughts or advice.

scribe.description: Captures key insights and themes that emerge, helping the group remember what was shared.

practising.rotation: Crucially, these roles rotate. Everyone becomes a speaker, a listener, and a scribe after an allotted time. No one controls the outcome. Instead, we place faith in what can emerge when we listen together in love. As Proverbs 20:5 says, "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water,but a man of understanding will draw it out." This practice is a way of drawing out—not just others' words, but the meaning beneath them, even those meanings hidden from ourselves.
practising.discovery: As the conversation unfolds, it often leads us to discoveries none of us could have reached alone. As Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 13:12, "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known." Our understanding is always partial. But through mutual listening, we begin to uncover not only what we don't know, but what we don't know we don't know—the blind spots and assumptions that only another's voice can help illuminate.
practising.faith: This practice is not about asserting control over words or ideas, but about cultivating faith in the conversation itself—faith that when we "submit to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21), something deeper than individual insight can emerge. We begin, as 2 Timothy 2:24–25 teaches, to "patiently endure," "correct with gentleness," and leave room for "God [to] grant them [or us!] repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth."

guideCta.title: Want to learn more about these roles?
guideCta.description: Download our detailed guide to understand each role deeply and prepare for meaningful conversations.

format.intro1: The specific structure—Speaker, Listener, Scribe—has no direct precedent in Scripture, it is a newer technology. But many of our current practices are. The early church had no hymn books, Sunday schools, or digital tools. We use these because they help us live out the principles of Scripture.
format.intro2: This listening format is just that—a tool to enact timeless values:

humility.title: Humility
humility.verse: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.

mutualSubmission.title: Mutual Submission
mutualSubmission.verse: Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.

drawingWisdom.title: Drawing Out Wisdom
drawingWisdom.verse: The purposes of a person's heart are deep waters, but one who has insight draws them out.

pitfalls.title: It also helps us guard against common pitfalls:

items.reactiveness: Reactiveness and debate: The Listener doesn't reply, but reflects back what they heard.
items.dominance: Dominance and status: The roles rotate—no one stays in charge.
items.losingInsight: Losing insight: The Scribe helps capture what might otherwise be forgotten or overlooked.

format.grounding: This structure is a modern method, but by testing its spirit—discerning whether it aligns with godly wisdom—we find it grounded in Scripture. We are not seeking novelty for its own sake, but new ways to become what we are called to be: a people shaped by love, wisdom, and deep mutual care.
format.discernment: Some may worry that careful listening opens us to harmful or misleading ideas. But to listen is not to agree. In Genesis 3:17 Adam is critiqued for listening to his wife and disobeying God—not for hearing her words, but for giving them authority over God's command. In other cases, like Rehoboam (1 Kings 12), the failure was choosing the wrong advisers. Scripture calls us to test what we hear, not to fear hearing it. Structured listening creates space to slow down, reflect, and weigh words against Scripture so that weak reasoning is realised and self-correction becomes possible. Even in more homogeneous groups, reflecting ideas back accurately and inviting gentle challenge can surface Scripture-shaped discernment and reduce reactive misunderstanding, helping the body grow in truth and love.

protections.title: Why this structure protects against error:

items.trust: Unlike debate, the space given to an idea builds trust; having been heard, proponents are more likely to receive correction during others' speaking time. The practice creates better conditions for correction by building trust first.
items.selfCorrection: Ideas are drawn out and explored more completely, making flaws more apparent to the speaker or to others who can respond in their turn. The practice helps people self-correct, which is often more effective than external correction.
items.smallGroups: Discussion occurs in smaller groups, allowing exploration and testing of ideas without involving everyone.
items.scribing: Reflection and scribing create accountability and preserve clarity, preventing misleading claims, as well as good insights from going unnoticed.
items.pace: The slowed pace and rotation of roles encourage discernment, humility, trust, and careful evaluation, helping participants move beyond initial emotional reactions to more thoughtful consideration.
items.timeLimits: Time limits bring balance, preventing any one idea from overwhelming the group.

rootedInWord.title: Rooted in the Word
rootedInWord.content: We are grounding this approach in Scripture. We believe listening is not just a communication skill; it's a spiritual practice. It aligns with the gentleness and patience Paul urged in 2 Timothy. It creates the conditions where we may correct without quarrelling, and teach without pride. It is the soil in which love, patience, and mutual forbearance can grow.
